title: Rollout-Time Intervention:Unlocking Agentic Reinforcement Learning Beyond Policy Limits

paper.title: Rollout-Time Intervention: Unlocking Agentic Reinforcement Learning Beyond Policy Limits
paper.abstract:
Abstract Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a key paradigm for improving large language model (LLM) agents, enabling stronger reasoning, planning, and tool-use in interactive environments. However, existing agent RL methods remain fundamentally constrained by an on-policy reasoning bottleneck: when tasks exceed the model’s current capability boundary, effective trajectories become extremely sparse and training often collapses.
We introduce Rollout-Time Intervention (RTI) , a technique designed to elicit successful trajectories beyond the policy’s intrinsic exploration capacity.
RTI operates by leveraging reward-side evidence (i.e., evaluation rubrics) during rollout to convert erroneous trajectories into successful ones, providing effective learning signals for tasks that the policy rarely solves on its own.
Although intervention trajectories are inherently off-policy, we find that they can effectively guide policy optimization when trajectories with excessive distributional shifts are filtered out.
Extensive experiments across five benchmarks demonstrate that RTI consistently outperforms RL baselines, enabling the post-trained policy to approach the performance of substantially stronger contemporary LLMs and, more importantly, transcend its original capability boundary.
The code is available at https://github.com/Alibaba-NLP/qqr .

The code is available at https://github.com/Alibaba-NLP/qqr . 1 Introduction LLMs are rapidly evolving from static instruction-following systems into interactive agents that can collaborate with external environments to achieve goals ( Team, 2026 ; Froger et al., 2025 ) . RL has been a key driver of this shift, enabling advanced capabilities such as self-reflection and long-horizon planning ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Qian et al., 2026 ) . These advances have fueled strong performance in challenging agent settings, including mathematical reasoning with code interpreters ( Feng et al., 2025 ) , deep research with search engines ( Jin et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2026 ) , and complex real-world tool use ( Qian et al., 2026 ; Gao et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026 ; Dong et al., 2026b ; Li et al., 2026 ) . Figure 1: RTI enables successful trajectories where on-policy and teacher-guided RL fail. Nevertheless, standard RL is limited by its on-policy nature: it mainly amplifies behaviors already supported by the current policy, rather than inducing new reasoning patterns ( Zhao et al., 2025 ; Yue et al., 2026 ) . As a result, when tasks lie beyond the model’s capability boundary, successful trajectories become extremely sparse, leading to unstable training or even collapse (Figure 1 (a)). Teacher-guided methods such as LUFFY ( Yan et al., 2026 ) and OPD ( Lu & Thinking Machines Lab, 2025 ) can partially mitigate this issue, but their improvements remain bounded by teacher capability. To further understand these failures, we examine failed agent trajectories and find a recurring pattern: the agent often possesses the knowledge and tools needed to complete the task, but makes a small early reasoning or action error at a task-critical step. As illustrated in Figure 1 , in τ 2 \tau^{2} -Telecom, the agent must guide the user to invoke a user-side tool, yet the model may incorrectly treat it as an agent-accessible tool and repeatedly attempt to call it; in Navigation, user queries are often ambiguous, and the agent must interpret noisy POI search results in the context of the user’s intent rather than blindly treating a returned POI as the target. In both cases, a single incorrect interaction strategy can steer subsequent reasoning into a failure loop, while correcting this early decision is often sufficient for the remaining trajectory to proceed normally. These observations motivate us: if such early reasoning errors can be corrected so that the rollout succeeds, can RL learn from these corrected trajectories and thereby push the policy beyond its original reasoning limits (Figure 1 (c))? However, such intervention introduces a central technical challenge: the corrected trajectories are no longer sampled from the original policy, but generated by an intervention-induced behavior policy. This discrepancy poses two fundamental risks. First, privileged reward-side information may leak into the reasoning process, producing shortcut-driven or behaviorally implausible trajectories that could not arise under genuine task interaction. Second, intervention may induce substantial distributional shifts from the original policy. In PPO-style optimization, including GRPO, such shifts can push importance ratios beyond the clipping range, suppressing otherwise useful learning signals, while low-probability actions may yield high-variance gradients that destabilize training. To this end, we propose Rollout-Time Intervention (RTI) , comprising three components: (1) reward-aware multi-agent intervention , which employs a Validator–Corrector–Verifier pipeline to transform failed rollouts into successful intervention trajectories while preventing privileged-information leakage; (2) perplexity-based distribution gating , which filters intervened trajectories that deviate excessively from the current policy; and (3) reasoning-shift-aware token reweighting , which concentrates policy updates on critical tokens where intervention induces substantial strategy changes. Together, these components enable stable learning from successful trajectories beyond the policy’s unaided exploration capacity, thereby pushing the policy beyond its original capability boundary. Experiments on public and real-world benchmarks show that RTI substantially outperforms baselines and achieves a breakthrough in the boundaries of reasoning capabilities. 2 Related Work Agentic Reasoning for LLMs. Agentic reasoning reframes LLMs as autonomous agents that combine planning, acting, and learning through interaction ( Wei et al., 2026 ) , as exemplified by ReAct ( Yao et al., 2023 ) , tool-use and search-based agents, and workflow-oriented systems with verifiable sub-tasks ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Jin et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2026 ; Feng et al., 2025 ) . This paradigm requires agents to plan over long horizons, navigate partial observability, and actively improve through feedback ( Wang et al., 2024 ) . Existing methods for agent training are as follows: (i) Data-synthesis-driven SFT improves tool use by generating interaction trajectories for supervised fine-tuning, including ToolLLM ( Qin et al., 2024 ) , ToolACE ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , APIGen-MT ( Prabhakar et al., 2026 ) , TopoCurate ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , and simulation or self-evolving pipelines for multi-turn data generation ( Li et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2026 ) . These methods are effective but depend on large-scale trajectory synthesis. (ii) Pure RL with verifiable rewards has also shown promise when outcomes are easy to verify. ReTool ( Feng et al., 2025 ) incorporates code execution for competition-level problem solving, Search-R1 ( Jin et al., 2025 ) learns search-engine use with emergent multi-query behavior, ZeroSearch ( Sun et al., 2026 ) replaces real retrieval with LLM simulation, and ToolRL ( Qian et al., 2026 ) shows that fine-grained format and outcome rewards can support stable multi-step tool-use RL. More recently, AEPO ( Dong et al., 2026a ) further improves optimization stability under long-horizon, multi-turn tool use through entropy-aware policy updates. Teacher-Guided Training for LLMs. When tasks lie beyond the model’s capability boundary, successful rollouts become extremely sparse and the policy is rarely exposed to truly corrective trajectories. To alleviate this, recent work studies teacher-guided training in two forms. One line provides token-level credit assignment using stronger teachers, often via trajectory-level teacher-student KL to derive dense rewards ( Gu et al., 2024 ; Lu & Thinking Machines Lab, 2025 ) . Another line introduces off-policy successful trajectories : LUFFY ( Yan et al., 2026 ) , for instance, combines offline expert data with online rollouts and uses importance sampling to handle distribution shift. While these methods can improve exploration and learning, they all fundamentally depend on stronger teacher models, making their gains bounded by the teacher’s capability ceiling. 3 Preliminaries Problem Setting. We formulate the agentic task as a trajectory generation problem. Let 𝒯 \mathcal{T} denote the set of tools. Given a query x x sampled from a task distribution 𝒟 \mathcal{D} , the policy π θ \pi_{\theta} produces a multi-step interaction trajectory τ \tau consisting of interleaved chain-of-thought reasoning z k z_{k} , tool invocations a k ∈ 𝒯 a_{k}\in\mathcal{T} , environmental feedback o k o_{k} , and a final answer y y : τ = [ z 1 , a 1 , o 1 , … , z k , a k , o k , … , y ] \tau=[z_{1},a_{1},o_{1},\dots,z_{k},a_{k},o_{k},\dots,y] .
